claims.text: A blog post titled "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi" exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ and covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
AWS CDK tied infrastructure to AWS.
Multi-cloud was nearly impossible with AWS CDK.
In its early days, SST was built on top of AWS CDK, which allowed developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
CDK and CloudFormation act as a code generator producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources.
AWS CDK is AWS-only, while Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-prem.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python, while Pulumi supports any programming language.
Pulumi deployments are faster than AWS CDK because of direct execution versus CloudFormation.
AWS CDK uses a CloudFormation state file, while Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
AWS CDK secrets management is limited to AWS Secrets Manager only, while Pulumi offers cross-cloud secret support.
Pulumi offers real-time debugging.
Pulumi supports custom providers and workflows for extensibility.
Pulumi executes infrastructure code directly during deployment rather than generating an intermediary format.

The SST Founding Engineer said: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
Pulumi Insights provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities.
Pulumi has built-in extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components.
Pulumi supports defining infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploying to AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments.
Pulumi Cloud Deployments documentation exists at /docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/ describing advanced deployment workflows.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies "day one" tasks, documented in the AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
An on-demand workshop titled "Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS" exists at pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications, in which constructs/components are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation.
Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3.
SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine, while also bridging Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service called SST Console; the Console is optional and includes a free tier.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud dependency; the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps its state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account (self-hosted), not in Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3 is the Ion-based rewrite of the SST framework.
The SST team has repeatedly stated, since the rewrite shipped, that SST is built on the Pulumi engine architecture.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack.
SST can deploy applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST apps define infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST components (functions, queues, buckets, static sites), and `sst deploy` handles provisioning.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite code-named Ion that replaced the entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported SST architecture since.

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
SST docs 'What is SST' say: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin's article 'Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis' says SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to be defined and deployed.

Kiryl Anoshka's dev.to article 'SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion' says: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

The published `platform/package.json` for SST depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`, plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds and more, alongside a Pulumiverse Vercel provider (`@pulumiverse/vercel`).

The SST repository has moved to `anomalyco/sst` (formerly `sst/sst`), and its platform/package.json lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies.

In SST's deploy chain, `sst deploy` reads sst.config.ts and resolves SST components, components compile into Pulumi resource declarations, the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs actual state, builds a dependency graph and orders operations, and Terraform-bridged providers translate resources into cloud API calls.
Pulumi's engine provides dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's provider ecosystem adapted for the Pulumi engine.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API works by embedding Pulumi programs inside teams' own tools, in the same embedded manner.
The Pulumi provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
The page /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/ and the blog post /blog/any-terraform-provider/ exist and cover Terraform providers.
Nitric and Defang, besides SST, also run application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building their own diff, state, and provider layer.
Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework whose docs state "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Official Nitric providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.

Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud, and its Pulumi provider (DefangLabs/pulumi-defang) is described as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`".
Nitric, Defang, and SST expose a narrower, more opinionated interface while relying on the Pulumi engine and provider bridge underneath.
Most SST users never write a line of Pulumi code; they work entirely in SST's component model.
Within an SST app, users can define raw Pulumi resources directly for resources without a dedicated SST construct and deploy them as part of the same app.
The latest SST release is v4.17.1, released in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package receives roughly 796,000 downloads a week (796,291 for the week of September 5-11, 2026).
SST's own team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has grown quickly since launch and now has more GitHub stars than SST.
SST's dependency on the Pulumi engine hasn't changed as opencode's prominence grew.
Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state, policy as code provides central guardrails, and Pulumi components enable sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state; its components are defined using Terraform providers bridged through the Pulumi engine.
opencode's growth hasn't changed SST's release cadence.
The linked pages exist: /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/, /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/, /blog/any-terraform-provider/, /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/.
SST is still shipping and its team is not abandoning it.

SST is a strong fit for an opinionated full-stack application framework; Pulumi directly makes more sense for cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across applications that SST doesn't expose.
